Data formats, the wire and the screens still change between versions, and nothing here is promised to keep working across them, so keep the city in a directory you can rebuild.

⚠️ **<!-- xtask:begin maturity:titled -->Alpha<!-- xtask:end -->。** <!-- xtask:begin workspace_version -->0.0.9<!-- xtask:end --> something and nothing 已经可用：它能从头到尾跑起一座城，User 可以把真活交给它。数据格式、协议和界面在版本之间仍会变，跨版本的一切都不保证继续可用，所以请把城放在一个可以重建的目录里。

V0.0.9是第一个离开pre-alpha的版本，按照我对于成熟度的判定，从这个版本开始可以试用了，sprawling正式离开纯开发阶段，并在功能新增上减速，将重心移向优化和调试。

这个版本的核心是修复了大量问题并设计了一我希望它足够简洁和实用的WebUI，在下个版本让它变得更简洁且实用，很能理解自定义UI的需求但目前只提供了修改theme.css（配色）和直接重做两个选项。我寻思，90%用户的需求可能就是把背景换成自己喜欢的图片/视频（甚至项目有ffmpeg），所以目前在纠结下个版本（或者说V0.1.0Beta版）是将其实现还是直接快进到提供生成式UI的方案，这就不是WebUI+壁纸引擎而是另一种体验了。我的确想要做一个我认为足够好的UI并在此之外再提供自由度（打磨优质的香草冰淇淋口感和提供其他口味的冰淇淋也不冲突，自由度同时也包含开发的便利）。同时我将尽可能确保项目的向后兼容性即现在各种TOML/JSONL/Markdown文件不会因为未来的更新而导致需要重设计/无法读取。另外一个本版没办法做的问题是完整的性能读数，我想要测试主要功能的P50和P999，但近两天因为各种原因电脑总是重启，无法测试。严格来说我最近几个版本推进的内容已经和一开始关注的内容分开了，在一开始我在意的是多Agent之间的自由交流和长时间运行中的上下文管理和涌现性的哲学问题，而现在我则更多思考信息的匮乏、充分与过剩的状态（无论是UX还是AX）以及运行时性能，直到目前这个版本我一直在使用Pi+社区插件来构建sprawling，但我在不断提升强度的工作中逐渐开始意识到其极简主义设计并没有带来极简主义应有的表现。我们每天要进行几万次乃至更多的工具调用，如果每一次都积累一个微小的卡顿或每个Session在上下文过半后都占用相当大的RAM，一觉醒来就有可能拉出数个检查点的时间差异。另外一边我们今年已经见过了无数Harness或流氓软件开始窃取我们电脑上的key/git历史，现在不是作为一个开源软件去说因为我没有服务器所以不搜集用户隐私的时候而是正因我们是开源软件因而有必要帮你把key加密存储以确保Agent不会将其获取。某种程度上来说，越极简主义的系统的确运行地更快，但我们运行在具体的系统上，每个人遇到的瓶颈因为系统不同而不同，有时需要额外地做一些事情来确保运行"看起来正常"，你可以看到一段zig写的CPU亲和性调度代码用于减少堵车问题，具体细节请看对应的代码和文档，现在它还不是很”智能“，我希望你能在你的设备上实测然后告诉我如何优化它，或者单纯告诉我你的感受如何。在我思考”experience“这个概念时，我认为最有挑战性的是设计一个Mayor，严格来说目前所有的大厂都有做Code/Work/Personal的三分，例如Code保留在CLI，Work做一个GUI或者升级Chat，然后Personal就类似于Muse，Grok Bot，Dots这些。但现实是，所有的Work产品都很失败，本质Chat+SKILL+几个常用插件，而Agent时代Chat逐渐向云Agent演变（如果你不知道的话，Chat端依靠丢弃thinking块和上下文资料实现低成本长上下文，代价是一致性和深度大幅受限），CLI的Coding Harness或者IDE的内置Agent一个比一个强但在处理大量的工作而非只编程的时候就不够好了，至于个人Agent大部分应该都是套餐额度削减之后没办法被厂家逼着试用的，当我的工作娱乐消费全部绑定在一个入口的时候，我可太知道怎么投放广告了（想象一下手机开屏广告+扫脸支付的一个更糟糕版本）。但难道这三个功能相互冲突吗？我不觉得，分一个用于处理Office文件的工作区配上对应的SKILL/MCP和一个用于全局管理的Session，三个问题都解决了。我非常在意自己的想法，准确点说，我很重视我自己在面对问题时的思考，但管理多个Agent会天然把人带入一种ADHD的情况中会让我几乎无法思考，当后台有着各种任务正在进行的时候，我需要一个天生适合”精神分裂“或者说”多线程“的Agent来帮我专注于思考，所以Mayor的设计和WebUI的不少细节都是为了这个。当然，我看到了无数人在犯着一个严重的错误：给Agent一个通用身份。这件事的轻度版本是你是一个顶级/前沿设计师，重度版本则是直接让Agent去Cos一个固定的角色（比如我看到很多人就在自己的AGENTS.md里面写上你是鲸鱼娘，或者用英文写几个关键词说是”指令’），当你在玩Cosplay的时候当然没问题，但实际工作中只会让输出劣化，说“你是一个顶级设计师‘只是让Agent去Cos顶级设计师而不是让它的交付物像一个顶级设计师的交付物。

本来这个版本应该有”欢迎来到Night City！“这样的赛博风标记，尤其考虑到这是个非常”城市“的项目。正如上文说我在思考信息量的问题，更具体一些就是复杂性的问题，我们已经被功能主义设计教导“最好的设计就是让人感觉到没有设计，但没有设计在任何情况下都不等于不设计，相反是一种极度设计，只不过尽可能考虑到了折叠复杂性。something就是那些复杂性，被选出来的东西，而nothing就是被折叠的复杂性，或者说没有感觉的感觉，这一个月几乎就是在不断思考什么是something什么是nothing的不断拉扯，比如一开始的sprawling有一个redb的KV数据库，后面又考虑引入SQL数据库，但现在这两个都不在项目中。同时安装便利性也得到了优化，相比于直接下载release的压缩包，通过npm（更推荐bun）和crates.io（即cargo）下载更加方便，同时目前的版本更新检测也是基于npm和crates.io，发布release后也会最快速同步。

顺带一提，如果你想到了，something and nothing是杀人考察(前)的BGM。

向后兼容我尽量守：这一版的账本事件日志版本还是 2，新加的字段全是可选的，0.0.8 写下的账本一行都不用重写；协议这边从 WIRE_V 46 一路走到 56，改形了十次，老标签页会被明确拒绝而不是读错。

大小核这块这一版收得比较完整：那段 zig 只负责读机器（档位、处理器组、缓存组、我能不能用），读回来交给一个纯函数算计划；座位分成两个池，账本线程和视图折叠占计划末尾，其余给每个 run 的 lane，tokio worker 不再占着座位；每个 run 的编译进程在 Windows 上有 job 权重、在 Linux 上有 cgroup 的 cpu.weight（委派不了就只剩 nice 10）、在 macOS 上被压到 utility。还没量出来的是它到底值多少，这在上面的清单里。

以下是本版未完成事物的列表:

- 四臂对照的读数一次都没有：主要功能的 p50/p99/p999、每个 run 的份额到底让重负载下的等待少了多少、一步计算中途换核的次数。机器没能连续跑满一轮测量，所以 `[core] placement` 的缺省 `"soft"` 是设计支持的，不是读数定的。
- 第四臂 `pinned` 还差一步：Windows 上每个 run 的 job 取「余下处理器」掩码要由建 job 的那一处（`runtime::backlog::jobs`）设，而 `runtime` 不能依赖 `sprawling`，所以要先加一条把掩码交进 `Backlog` 的缝。今天 run 的进程因此离开 harness 的 job，落在操作系统手里，不比 `"soft"` 差，但不是完整的第四臂。
- 存储里还有几处整段读：`jsonl/open.rs` 的 `recover_tail` 与另外两条读路径会把预分配段的零尾一起读进来，打开一座预分配过的城要多读几十 MiB。
- 沙箱的 `native` 臂（Windows 的 Job Object + AppContainer、Linux 的 bwrap、macOS 的 Seatbelt）、skill 审计的实际执行者、按 run 的内存上限在 macOS 上的对应物，都还只是名字与规格。

**In English / 英文版**

What this version is for: this is the version that leaves pre-alpha. By the maturity ladder above, sprawling is usable from here, the project leaves pure development, new features slow down, and the work moves toward optimisation and debugging. By the maturity ladder above, sprawling is usable from here, and the project leaves pure development: fewer new features, and more of the work spent on making what exists faster, steadier and less surprising.

The core of this version is a large batch of fixes and the design of a WebUI I wanted simple and practical enough — the next version makes it simpler and more practical. I understand the wish for a custom UI, but today there are only two options: change `theme.css` (the colours) or rebuild it outright. My guess is that 90% of what people actually want is their own picture or video behind it (and the project already carries ffmpeg for that), so for the next version — or rather V0.1.0 Beta — I am torn between building that and skipping straight to a generative UI, which would not be a WebUI plus a wallpaper engine but another kind of experience altogether. I do want to make a UI I consider good enough and offer freedom on top of it (polishing a good vanilla and offering other flavours do not conflict, and freedom includes the convenience of developing against it). At the same time I will do what I can to keep the project backward compatible: the TOML/JSONL/Markdown files a city holds today should not need redesigning, or become unreadable, because of a later update. The other thing this version cannot do is a complete performance reading. I want the P50 and the P999 of the main features, and for the last few days this machine has kept restarting for one reason or another, so I could not measure. Strictly speaking, what I have pushed in the last several versions has drifted away from what I first cared about: at the start it was free conversation between agents, context management across long runs, and the philosophical question of emergence; now I think more about information being scarce, sufficient or excessive (in UX as much as in AX) and about runtime performance. Until this version I have been building sprawling with Pi plus community plugins, and as I pushed the intensity up I began to see that its minimalist design does not deliver what minimalism is supposed to deliver. We make tens of thousands of tool calls a day and more; if every one of them accumulates a small stall, or every session past the middle of its context holds a great deal of RAM, then a night's sleep can pull several checkpoints' worth of time difference apart. On the other side, we have seen any number of harnesses and outright rogue software this year start stealing the keys and the git history on our machines. This is not the moment to say, as an open-source project, that we collect nothing because we run no server; it is exactly because we are open source that it matters to keep your keys encrypted so that an agent cannot get at them. In a sense the more minimalist a system the faster it runs, but we run on concrete systems, everyone's bottleneck differs with the system, and sometimes extra work is what makes a run look normal. You can see a piece of Zig that schedules CPU affinity to cut down on traffic jams; the details are in the code and its documents. It is not very "smart" yet, and I would like you to measure it on your own machine and tell me how to improve it, or simply how it felt. In thinking about what "experience" means, the hardest thing I have found is designing a Mayor. Strictly speaking every large company has made the Code/Work/Personal split: Code stays in the CLI, Work gets a GUI or an upgraded Chat, and Personal looks like Muse, Grok Bot, Dots. The reality is that every Work product has failed — they are a Chat plus SKILLs plus a few common plugins — while in the agent era Chat is drifting toward a cloud agent (in case you do not know: the Chat side gets a cheap long context by discarding the thinking blocks and the context material, at the price of a large loss in consistency and depth). The CLI coding harnesses and the agents built into IDEs get stronger one after another, but they are not good enough when the work is a great deal of work rather than only programming; and as for personal agents, most of them are what you are pushed into trying after your plan's quota was cut. When my work, my entertainment and my spending all bind to one entrance, I know far too well how to place an advertisement (imagine a worse version of a phone's splash-screen ad plus face-scan payment). But do these three functions conflict with each other? I do not think so: one workspace for Office files with the SKILLs and MCP servers it needs, and one session for global management, and all three problems are solved. I care a great deal about my own thinking — more precisely, I care about how I think when I face a problem — but managing several agents puts a person into a state of ADHD that makes thinking nearly impossible, and when tasks are running in the background I need an agent that is born suited to being "split" or "multi-threaded" so that I can stay on my thinking. That is what the Mayor's design, and no small number of the WebUI's details, are for. Of course I have seen any number of people make one serious mistake: giving an agent a generic identity. The mild version is "you are a top-tier / frontier designer"; the severe version is having the agent cosplay a fixed role (I have seen people write "you are a whale girl" into their AGENTS.md, or a few English keywords called an "instruction"). Cosplay is fine when you are playing, but in real work it only degrades the output: saying "you are a top designer" only makes the agent cosplay a top designer, it does not make what it delivers look like what a top designer would deliver.

This version should have carried a mark like "Welcome to Night City!", the cyberpunk touch, especially for a project that is so much about a city. As I said above, I am thinking about how much information there is, which is more concretely a question about complexity. Functionalist design taught us that the best design is the design you do not notice, but design you do not notice never means no design in any situation; it is an extreme degree of design that has folded the complexity away as far as it can. something is that complexity, the things chosen; nothing is the complexity folded away, or a feeling with no feeling to it. This month has been one long tug of war over what is something and what is nothing: sprawling began with a redb KV database, later I considered bringing in SQL, and today neither is in the project. Installing got easier too: rather than downloading the release archive, npm (bun preferred) and crates.io (that is, cargo) are more convenient, and the update check is based on npm and crates.io today, so it syncs as fast as the release is published.

By the way, in case you thought of it: something and nothing is the BGM of 殺人考察(前).

On backward compatibility I hold the line as far as I can: the ledger's event-log version is still 2, every field this version adds is optional, and a ledger 0.0.8 wrote reads back line for line. The wire is another matter — it walked from WIRE_V 46 to 56, ten changes of shape, and an old browser tab is refused outright rather than misread.

The big-core/small-core side came together more completely this version: that piece of Zig only reads the machine (the classes, the processor groups, the cache groups, whether I may use a processor) and hands the reading to a pure function that works out a plan; the seats are two pools, the accounting thread and the view fold holding the plan's last ones and the rest going to each run's lane, with the tokio workers no longer holding one at all; each run's compilers get a job weight on Windows, a cgroup cpu.weight on Linux (nice 10 alone where the cgroup is not delegated), and utility QoS on macOS. How much any of that is worth is not measured yet, and that is in the list above.

What this version has not finished:

- Not one reading of the four-arm comparison: the p50/p99/p999 of the main features, how much the per-run shares actually cut the waits under heavy load, and how many times a step of work changed core mid-step. The machine never stayed up for one whole measurement, so the default `[core] placement = "soft"` is supported by the design rather than settled by a reading.
- The fourth arm, `pinned`, is one step short: on Windows each run's job has to take the mask of the remaining processors, and the place that makes a run's job (`runtime::backlog::jobs`) is in `runtime`, which may not depend on `sprawling`. So a seam handing the mask into `Backlog` comes first. Today a run's processes therefore leave the harness's job and land in the operating system's hands — no worse than `"soft"`, but not the whole fourth arm.
- Storage still reads whole segments in a few places: `recover_tail` in `jsonl/open.rs` and two other read paths bring a preallocated segment's zero tail in with the records, so opening a city that was preallocated reads tens of MiB more than it needs.
- The sandbox's `native` arm (Windows' Job Object with AppContainer, Linux's bwrap, macOS' Seatbelt), the auditor that actually runs a skill audit, and the macOS counterpart of the per-run memory limit are names and specifications only.

**Maturity ladder / 成熟度阶梯**

| Stage | Version | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pre-alpha | 0.0.x | runs end to end; nothing is promised |
| alpha | 0.0.x | usable / 可用 |
| beta | 0.1.0 | good to use / 好用 |
| stable | 1.0.0 | no compromise on experience or on long-term maintenance, with a mature maintainer or team / 体验与长期维护都不妥协，维护者或团队成熟 |
